resources.string: Churn
Before you start

Churn rewrites your router\'s IMEIs. Rewriting an IMEI is a criminal offense in some countries, for example under the UK\'s Mobile Telephones (Re-programming) Act 2002. Check the law where you use the router.
Churn only protects you if you follow its rules every time. You can read them again from the router screen.
I understand
Rules
Each card\'s network records where and when the card was used. Churn\'s new IMEIs keep these records apart, and the rules keep everything else from tying them to each other or to you.

A card here is a normal SIM card or an eSIM adapter card, and Churn knows two kinds. A travel card is used on the go and never again once you\'ve swapped it out. A place card is a new card for one place you return to, other than home and work, and you use it there on every visit and nowhere else.
Always follow these rules:

string-array.name: rules_always
string-array.item: Switch the router off before you get home, to work or to any other place you return to, and keep it switched off or without a card there. The only exception is a place card at its own place.

Before you leave home or work with the router, remove the SIM card or disable the eSIM profile in every phone, tablet, watch or laptop you carry, and keep it that way until you\'re back home or at work.

Use the router only with devices that run Linux, or an Android system built for privacy, such as GrapheneOS. That rules out Windows, macOS, iPhones, iPads, Chromebooks and the Android that most phones and tablets come with.
Connect to the router by cable only, and keep its Wi-Fi off.
Send all traffic through the router\'s VPN, and don\'t use the router without it.
Put cards only into the SIM 2 tray, never put a second profile on an eSIM adapter card, and don\'t use the router\'s built-in eSIM.

Start each swap right after you\'re done with the old card, before you switch the router off. If you\'ve switched it off already, take the old card out before you switch it on again, and start the swap well away from home, work and any other place you return to. Switch the new card on later, and somewhere else.
Once you\'ve swapped out a travel card, destroy it away from home. If you run out of new cards, keep using the current one until you get a new one.

resources.string: For maximum privacy, also follow these rules where you can:

string-array.name: rules_where_you_can
string-array.item: Use cards that aren\'t registered to your name.
Get each new card from a different provider than the last one and than your place cards. If you can\'t, start using it somewhere else and some days after you stopped using the last one.
Vary when you swap cards, and where you switch the radio on and off.
Pay for the VPN in a way that isn\'t tied to your name.
Block the SIM 1 tray, for example with a drop of hot glue.

Set up the router

Churn keeps a folder on the router, /etc/churn/, with the router's IMEIs as its factory IMEIs and a script that writes them back. At every swap it also records the new card there, with the random IMEIs the card gets. A firmware upgrade that keeps settings keeps the folder; a factory reset deletes it.

Churn also keeps GL's system log, which records each SIM card's ICCID and IMSI and the cells it used, in memory only, so it is gone at every power-off. It deletes the saved log and removes all but the current card from GL's records. At your first swap it also overwrites the router's free storage, which takes a few minutes, so that what it deleted can't be read back. It keeps the zeros as files, apart from 512 MB of free storage, so that later overwrites only need to fill those 512 MB.

A swap needs GL\'s scheduled reboot off, and it is on. Turn it off in GL\'s web interface, then tap Refresh. A reboot is a power-on, so with a SIM inside it registers wherever it happens.

Turn the Enhanced Kill Switch on
Churn turns GL\'s Enhanced Kill Switch on. Devices behind the router then reach the internet only through the VPN, and not at all while it is down.
Churn\'s firewall rules aren\'t on the router, so the router\'s own traffic can bypass the VPN (rule 5).
Add Churn\'s firewall rules

Churn adds firewall rules to the router. Over the SIM, only the VPN\'s own traffic then goes out. Everything else that would use the SIM, the router\'s own traffic included, goes through the VPN, and nowhere while it is down. The router also looks up names at the VPN\'s DNS server. The rules cover only the SIM, not an internet connection over Wi-Fi or the Ethernet port.\n\nRemoving Churn from this router removes the rules.
GL saves its system log on the router, with each SIM card\'s ICCID and IMSI and the cells it used. The log links your cards to each other and to places.
Clear the SIM history

Churn keeps GL\'s system log in memory only, deletes the saved log, removes all but the current card from GL\'s records and overwrites the router\'s free storage, so that what it deleted can\'t be read back. It keeps the zeros as files, apart from 512 MB of free storage, so that later overwrites only need to fill those 512 MB. This can take a few minutes.\n\nRemoving Churn from this router puts back GL\'s setting for saving the system log and deletes the zero files.

Step %1$d of 4
What Churn did in step %1$d:
Prepare the router

Churn turns airplane mode on, sets slot 2 to the built-in eSIM with no profile enabled, and shuts the router down. Keep the cable connected until the router is off. Have the new card with you: in step 2 you switch the router on again here.\n\nWhy: a card in slot 2 registers at every power-on, whatever airplane mode says, so the new card must stay off until it has its own IMEIs. While slot 2 is on the built-in eSIM, the card in the SIM 2 tray stays off.

The router still has its factory IMEIs, as at your first swap. If you used it at home or at work before Churn, you can run steps 1 to 3 there: the router keeps those IMEIs until step 3, and the new card stays off. Step 4 still happens at another place.
\"Power On with Charger\" is off in GL\'s settings. Otherwise plugging in a charger switches the router on, wherever you are.
Start
Swap the card

1. Wait until the router is off, then unplug the cable.
2. Take out the battery, take the old card out of the SIM 2 tray if it's still there, and put the new one in. Leave the SIM 1 tray empty.
3. Put the battery back.
4. Switch the router on where you ran step 1, and connect the cable with Churn open. Churn goes on as soon as the router shows up on the cable, or when you tap Continue.

Why: at power-on only the built-in eSIM's short bursts go out, with a test identity that is likely the same on every Mudi 7. They likely don't carry the router's IMEIs. If they do, those are still the old card's, which show nothing new where that card was just in use.

If you've had to leave, switch the router on only well away from home, work and any other place you return to (rule 7). If you keep the old card after all, it keeps the IMEIs Churn gave it.
Continue
The router hasn\'t been off since Churn shut it down, so the card can\'t have been swapped yet. If the router is still on, switch it off by hand, then follow the steps above.
The router is still on the cable, two minutes after Churn shut it down. If it is still on, switch it off by hand before you go on.
Give the new card its IMEIs

Churn checks that a WireGuard VPN is still set up, waits until the router\'s radio is off, checks that the SIM 1 tray is empty, turns the Enhanced Kill Switch on if it is off, adds its firewall rules if they\'re missing, sets slot 2 to the SIM 2 tray and reads the new card\'s ICCID. Unless you kept the old card, it then asks you about the new one, with slot 2 back on the built-in eSIM until you answer. It records the card with its IMEIs, the ones a place card had before or new random ones, and writes them. Then it clears the SIM history on the router, which takes a few minutes the first time and less after that, and shuts the router down. The radio stays off throughout.\n\nWhy: a card in the SIM 1 tray registers at every power-on, whatever airplane mode says, so at the next one it would go out with the new card and link the two. With the Enhanced Kill Switch on, devices\' traffic doesn\'t bypass the VPN, even while the VPN is down (rule 5). Churn\'s firewall rules do the same for the router\'s own traffic over the SIM, and let nothing but the VPN use the SIM. While slot 2 is on the built-in eSIM, the card stays off, even if the router is switched off and on before you answer. The router\'s record of earlier cards would link them to the new one.
The card in SIM 2 is your place card %1$s. Continue gives it the IMEIs it had before.

Is the card in SIM 2, ending in %1$s, a new card for one place you'll return to, other than home and work? Then it's a place card: Churn keeps its IMEIs on this phone and gives them back to it on every visit, and you use it only at that place.

Otherwise it's a travel card, which you don't use again once you've swapped it out.

Only a new card should become a place card: one you've used elsewhere would tie those places to this one.
Cancel sets slot 2 back to the built-in eSIM and shuts the router down, so that you can put in another card.

The router has the new card's IMEIs and is shutting down. Wait until it is off, then unplug the cable.

Switch it on again later, at another place and time (rule 7), and never at home, at work or another place you return to. At power-on the new card registers with the network, whatever airplane mode says. The radio then stays off until you turn airplane mode off, on the router's screen or in GL's web interface.

Why: the old card went quiet where you started the swap. If the new one starts where and when the old one stopped, the two are easy to match.

The router has the place card's IMEIs and is shutting down. Wait until it is off, then unplug the cable.

Switch it on again later, at the card's own place, and never anywhere else. At power-on the card registers with the network, whatever airplane mode says. The radio then stays off until you turn airplane mode off, on the router's screen or in GL's web interface.

Why: used only at its place, the card links nothing but your visits there (rule 1). The old card went quiet where you started the swap. If the new one starts when the old one stopped, the two are easy to match.

Dry run

The dry run runs steps 1 and 3 of a swap on a router with no SIM, as far as they go without one, and so confirms claims of docs/testing.md that only a change of the router\'s settings can. Both trays must be empty and no profile enabled on the built-in eSIM. The dry run keeps the radio off, writes a test pair of IMEIs, and puts slot 2, the active slot and the IMEIs back as they were. Like a swap, it turns airplane mode and the Enhanced Kill Switch on and puts Churn\'s firewall rules in place, and leaves them so. The debug log, if it is on, keeps every command.

The last dry run stopped before it put the router back as it was, so slot 2, the active slot or the IMEIs may still be as the dry run left them. Put the router back, or forget the dry run if you have put the router back yourself.

Back
Removal and clearing

The removal test runs Churn\'s restore.sh, as Remove Churn does, checks what it did, and sets the router up again as it was, with the card\'s record, the IMEIs it had and Churn\'s firewall rules. It then clears the SIM history twice, as step 3 does. It confirms claims of docs/testing.md about restore.sh and the clearing, and runs once for each firmware: restore.sh deletes the zero files, so the first clearing fills all of the flash\'s free space, about 2.9 GB, which takes minutes, as does reading all of the partition afterwards. No profile may be enabled on the built-in eSIM, and the SIM 1 tray must be empty. The test leaves airplane mode on. The debug log, if it is on, keeps every command.
restore.sh deletes Churn\'s folder, and the test then writes it anew. If the test stops in between, the router screen shows this screen until the router is set up again.

The last removal test stopped before it set the router up again, so the router may still have the factory IMEIs and no Churn folder or firewall rules. Set the router up again, or forget the test if you have set the router up yourself.
The removal test stopped while confirming %1$s.\n\n%2$s

Power cycles

The power cycle test shuts the router down twice and checks each power-on, which confirms claims of docs/testing.md that only a power-on can. You switch the router on again each time. Both trays must be empty: the test puts slot 2 on the SIM 2 tray, where the router emitted nothing at power-on with both trays empty. It saves a test pair of IMEIs across the first power-on, and at the end puts slot 2, the active slot and the IMEIs back as they were. Like a swap, it turns airplane mode and the Enhanced Kill Switch on and puts Churn\'s firewall rules in place, and leaves them so. The debug log, if it is on, keeps every command.
The test shuts the router down twice and waits for you to switch it on again each time. Until it has put the router back as it was, the router screen shows this screen.

Once the router is off, switch it on again with Churn open and both trays still empty. The test goes on as soon as the router shows up on the cable, or when you tap Go on. To put the router back as it was instead, tap Put the router back before you switch the router on.

Debug log

Churn can keep a log of what it does on the router, so that a problem can be looked into afterwards: each command it sends and the router\'s answer, what each step did and why it stopped, and what GL\'s eSIM manager logged during steps 1 and 3. The log leaves out ICCIDs, IMSIs and IMEIs, the contents of files, your VPN settings and the time of day, and keeps the last three swaps. It stays on this phone until you share it, and turning it off keeps it until you delete it.
